newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania markets unaffected by failed NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: Romania markets unaffected by failed NATO bid.

text.p: Romania's unsuccessful bid to win early NATO membership is unlikely to hit foreign capital inflows or affect markets as investors are more concerned by progress in implementing reforms, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Foreign investors to Romania are interested in internal rather than external politics," a Western analyst said. "Moreover, the news about non-admission was not a surpise."
"More and more foreigners are now taking an interest in emerging markets and in this sector Romania is a fine prospect with or without NATO membership," a local trader said.
A NATO summit in Madrid on Tuesday invited Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to join the Alliance and named Romania and Slovenia as deserving candidates for a 1999 review.
Romanian leaders have accepted the setback and pledged to pursue reforms to ensure admission by the turn of the century.

"Romania's nomination for 1999 was a good signal to foreign investors, showing it complied with European political, economic and military standards and had potential," said Creditanstalt Securities Romania President Marcel Cobuz. "Investors to Romania are now investing in that potential."

Foreign investors, absent from Romanian markets before the election last year of a centrist government, have rushed to Romanian equities. Volume and turnover levels have hit record levels on the stock exchange and the over-the-counter market.
The centrist government, which took office after seven years of rule by leftists, has pledged to back capital market growth and foreign investment.
Facing a review this month of its progress by the International Monetary Fund, the government has pressed ahead in the past week to meet its pledges for fast reforms.
Parliament last week approved a government decree on foreign investment, granting increased incentives and setting portfolio rules for the first time.

"It's not NATO that counts. Foreigners want to see the government delivering on its promises," a London broker said. "Investors will not react to being kept out of NATO. They want to see stability of the national leu currency and macro- economic stability in general," a local broker said.
The Romanian currency market was also unmoved by the Madrid decision, with the leu opening at 7,100/150 to the dollar -- about the level it has maintained for the past two weeks.
Creditanstalt Romania's Cobuz believed capital inflows would increase substantially towards the end of the year.

"As the region's second largest market Romania is promising now when there is a macro-economic depression syndrome in the Czech Republic, when listings in Hungary are not numerous and expensive and when investors do not know what to expect after elections in Poland in autumn," he added.
